title: Grove never claims Merkl rewards itself; it authorises an external operator to claim on the proxy's behalf
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.14 scopes the entire Merkl module to "manage the **operators authorized** to claim Merkl rewards on behalf of the Grove ALM Proxy" — there is no `claimMerkl` function at all. A...14.1.2 calls `toggleOperator` on the `MERKL_DISTRIBUTOR` through the proxy, and A...14.1.1 gates it on `RELAYER`.

Delegation rather than direct claiming reflects how Merkl works: entitlements are computed off-chain and claimed with a merkle proof, so the claim transaction needs data Grove's controller has no way to hold or validate on-chain. Rather than build a proof-passing interface, Grove grants a third party the right to claim into the proxy.

The layering is the interesting part. **Which distributor contract** is trusted is set by `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` via `setMerklDistributor` (A...3.1.9) — a governance decision, since the distributor could in principle be malicious. **Which operator** may act at that distributor is a relayer decision, revocable by the same toggle. Venue trust is governed; agent trust is operated.

As with the Ethena delegated signer (A...10.1), this is a capability grant with no quantitative control attached: `toggleOperator` carries no amount, so no rate limit can apply. The saving grace is that a Merkl operator can only claim rewards *into* the proxy, not move existing holdings out — the delegation is narrower than the Ethena one, which is why it warrants less concern despite the identical shape.
description: toggleOperatorMerkl is relayer-gated with no amount and no rate limit, while the distributor address it trusts is set only by DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE — trust in the venue and in the agent are separated.
